title: Clavinet and RMI keyboards: playing bass differently
summary: In San Francisco he built a group of RMI, clavinet, drums and bass to avoid sounding like a traditional bassist.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: I was in San Francisco. I had taken an instrument up, a clavinnet. Clavinets were new on the scene. But I heard something there that I wanted to be involved with. It was electronic, and I guess I was getting into electronics, but getting into them...not freaking out in them. Because I could see my...the sound I was striving for. I felt like that lent itself to it, to accompany what I was doing. Because I didn't want to play the bass like a bass. That's what made me altogether another kind of animal, and I knew that. But I...
...and that's the premise behind the bass method book that you put out?

Could be. Possibly, yeah, sure it is, behind everything I'm doing now. It's because I didn't want to sound like nobody else, not that anybody do. But the approach I was using for the instrument wasn't traditional. It was foreign to whatever...For example, I had two keyboards: the clavinnet and the RMI...

Right, because that was the instrument I heard that had the — closer — of the bigger notes in the left hand, rather than an organ to get the bottom, because I knew if I got away from the bottom with my bass, there was no bottom there. I needed something for bottom to give me a chance to go up on top. But I had the clavinnet to mix into the sound, so my group consisted of RMI, clavinnet, drums and bass. Now, that was an odd instrumentation.
